Local changes to the Biowasm runtime and programs in this folder
================================================================
Upstream: https://github.com/biowasm/biowasm (the programs and the base module) and
https://github.com/biowasm/aioli (the runner, aioli.js).

Every program here is the real program, compiled to WebAssembly. The changes below are what it
took to make them behave in a web page as they do on Linux: exit statuses, standard
input/output/error as real files, error messages, and output that is not lost.

The runner, the programs and these changes are the same as in the Bioinformatics workbench, from
which this site was made; that site has many more programs. Two parts of the runner were made
for programs that are not in this site: they are named below, and have no effect here.

1. aioli.js – the runner
------------------------
aioli.js is Aioli 3.2.3 as the Biowasm CDN serves it (https://biowasm.com/cdn/v3/aioli.js: the file
dist/aioli.js of the npm package @biowasm/aioli 3.2.3 with one comment line at the top), with the
three changes a–c below. Compared with that file on 15 October 2026, nothing else differs.

a. A method execIO was added to Aioli's worker. It runs one program with standard input, output
   and error bound to real file descriptors, and returns the program's exit status.
   execio-source.txt is its readable source (in aioli.js the worker is one long encoded string).
   In execIO:
   - Before each run the program's view of the shared folder (/shared, PROXYFS) is mounted
     again, so that a file another program deleted and made again is not served from a stale
     cache of names.
   - After each run the program's module is started afresh, as a process is on Linux. A module
     that stays keeps its C globals from one run to the next: getopt's state, for one.
     (Upstream starts only some programs afresh; here it is every program. The base module,
     which holds the files, stays.)
   - Starting a program afresh needs no network. In _setup, which sets a program up, the
     program's loader is read once and its factory is kept; its .wasm file is compiled once and
     the compiled module is kept (each start makes a new instance of it, with new memory); a
     .data package, for a program that has one, is kept in memory after the first start (none of
     the programs here has one). Upstream fetches the files again for every start – from the
     browser's cache while that is fresh, and from the server once it is stale (after ten
     minutes on GitHub Pages) – so that every command needed the network, and stopped working
     when the connection dropped.
   - Only the program that is asked for is set up. One that cannot be loaded (the connection is
     gone at its first use) reports that, does not stop the other programs, and is tried again
     the next time. If the start afresh after a run fails, the run's result is still returned.
   - The shared file system gets a function fstat, which the file-system proxy (PROXYFS) of an
     older Emscripten calls when a file is opened for appending (Emscripten bug 12367; Biowasm's
     build script replaces that call in its loaders where it has the form the script looks for).
     It was added for fastp, a program of the Bioinformatics workbench; none of the loaders here
     calls it, and it has no effect here.
   - The errors of the shared file system get their names (ENOENT, EACCES …). Each program has
     its own copy of Emscripten's file-system code and recognises a foreign error only by
     name; without the names a program that asked about a missing file with stat() or
     access() stopped with "abort(Error: FS error)" – "sort no_such_file" did. Now it prints
     its own message.
   - After main() returns, fflush(0) is called where the program's loader offers it as
     Module._fflush. That too was added for fastp; none of the loaders here offers it, and it
     has no effect here.
   - "2>&1" opens standard output and standard error on the same file for appending.
   - The links that the page hands over (io.links) are made in the program's file system. The
     page hands over one: /home/user (the home folder) -> the folder of the shared file system
     that holds the student's files (/shared/vfs/home/user; see assets/js/tools-wasm.js). Paths
     in the home folder therefore reach the programs as they were typed, and the programs print
     them as typed (md5sum's output, grep -H, the headers of diff -u). There is no link /data:
     the data files of this site are copied into the home folder (~/data) on a first visit
     (data/PROVENANCE.md at the top of the site).
   - A run reports how much of its standard input the program read: where the program left
     the input (stdinPos – after "head -n 1": behind the first line) and the furthest byte it
     read (stdinMax – what a program takes from a pipe, where it cannot go back). The shell
     needs this for a program that stands in a block, a function or a script with redirected
     input ({ head -n 1; sort; } < FILE, f() { wc -l; }; f < FILE): what the program did not
     read is the input of the next command, and a program that does not read at all
     (while read x; do grep -c "$x" table.csv; done < LIST) leaves the list to the loop.
   - A run reports in which order the program wrote to its standard output and to its standard
     error (which of the two, and how many bytes, in turn). Where both go the same way – to the
     terminal, or into the file of a script that was started with "> log.txt 2>&1" – the page
     passes them on in that order: "wc -l a.txt nosuch b.txt" prints the count of a.txt, then the
     message about the missing file, then the count of b.txt, as on Linux. What a program keeps
     in the C library's buffer until it ends is written when it ends, as on Linux when the
     output is not a terminal.
   - A run can have the clock of another time zone, and the time zone has its short name.
     Emscripten takes the time zone from the browser and takes no notice of TZ: "date -u" printed
     the local time with a Z behind it, and the zone as "British Summer Time". For "date -u",
     "TZ=UTC date" and "TZ=America/New_York date" the page asks for the clock of that zone (the
     JavaScript Date that the program's runtime uses gives the time of that zone for the length
     of the run; any zone that the browser knows by its name – Europe/Paris, Asia/Tokyo). "date"
     prints BST, CEST, EDT … where the browser knows the short name; TZ=GMT is called GMT.
     (For dates of the years 1968 to 1971 in the United Kingdom, date here prints GMT where a
     Linux computer prints BST: clocks were one hour ahead all year then.) The page asks for
     this clock for date, for awk (strftime, mktime) and for diff (the file times in the headers
     of diff -u and diff -c).
   - The input of a program can be handed over a line at a time. sed in a block whose input is
     a file ({ sed 1q; cat; } < FILE) must leave what it did not use to the next command; on
     Linux the C library puts the rest back when sed ends, here sed never gets more than the
     line it is at. (Only then: every other run reads as much as it asks for.)
   - /dev/zero is there for the programs (head -c 1000 /dev/zero > FILE). Emscripten has
     /dev/null, /dev/random and /dev/urandom, and no /dev/zero.
   - The environment of the shell reaches the programs. Emscripten gives every program the
     same made-up environment (USER=web_user, HOME=/home/web_user, LANG from the browser),
     built when the program is set up, from a table that nothing outside the program's loader
     can reach: awk's ENVIRON showed that, and "export NAME=value" or "LC_ALL=C sort" changed
     nothing. Now room is kept behind a program's environment when the program is set up (in
     _setup: the two functions through which the C library asks for the environment,
     environ_sizes_get and environ_get, are wrapped – found by their names, also in loaders that
     have shortened the names of their imports), and before each run execIO writes the
     variables that the page hands over (io.env, a list of NAME=value) into that room: up to
     1,000 variables and 128 KiB. The page hands over what the shell exports
     (assets/js/tools-wasm.js, envOf). A program that does not ask for its environment is not
     touched; every program here asks for it.
   - A program can be told that its standard input is a pipe (io.fifo). Here a pipe is a file,
     and a program that asks what its input is – fstat() – learns that it is a regular file.
     GNU wc sets the width of its columns by that: "cat f | wc" prints "      3       3      17"
     on Linux and printed " 3  3 17" here. With io.fifo the file that is the program's input
     answers that it is a pipe. The page sets it for wc only – every other program reads its
     input as before.
   - A file that a program renames over another file leaves no ghost behind. "sed -i" writes a
     temporary file and renames it to the name of the file it edits. The shared file system is
     that of an older Emscripten, whose rename takes the renamed file out of its table of names
     and puts it back under the new name – but leaves the file that had that name before in the
     table. While the new file is there, it is found first. Once it is removed (rm, mv), the old
     one is found again: for every program the file was "there" with the contents from before
     the edit, although no folder listed it, and what programs then wrote under that name went
     into the ghost and was lost. (Later versions of Emscripten remove the overwritten file in
     rename.) Now the rename of the shared file system is wrapped: the file that was at the new
     name before is taken out of the table.
   - A program that renames a file does not leave the old NAME behind either. Each program sees
     the shared file system through a proxy of its own (PROXYFS, again of an older Emscripten).
     Its rename hands the work on – and does not give the proxy's own node its new name, so that
     the node went back into the proxy's table under the OLD name: for the rest of that run the
     old name counted as taken. "sed -i" renames a temporary file into place for every file it
     edits, and the C library of these builds (musl) names temporary files after the clock: two
     files handled within one tick got the same name, the second "existed", and after 100 tries
     sed gave up – "couldn't open temporary file ./sedXXXXXX: File exists", status 4, the
     remaining files not edited ("sed -i 's/a/b/' *.txt" with many small files failed more
     often than not). Now each program's proxy is wrapped once: after its rename the node has
     its new name and folder, as in later versions of Emscripten.
b. A method statTree was added to Aioli's worker. It answers, in one message, what is in the
   shared file system below a folder: path, size, time of the last change and whether it is a
   folder, for every entry. Before and after each program the page compares the programs' files
   with its own; asked file by file – one message each – that took a second longer per program
   in a folder of a thousand files. (Its source is in execio-source.txt too.)
c. In the main-thread part of aioli.js the worker is kept as Aioli.lastWorker, so that the page
   can stop a program that does not end (Ctrl+C twice in the terminal) by ending the worker.

The page gives Aioli the base module (base/1.0.0) as the first tool: Aioli keeps the shared
file system in the first one, and the programs that are started afresh must not own it.
(That is in assets/js/tools-wasm.js, not a change to aioli.js.)

2. JavaScript loaders – NAME.js next to each NAME.wasm
------------------------------------------------------
In the loader of every program, exit(status) is recorded as Module.__exitStatus. The loaders of
the 17 coreutils programs, gawk, grep 3.7 and sed were changed for this; the loaders of the
programs that were compiled for the course – diff, cmp and grep-perl – get it from their build
scripts, which also give the programs their names (diff, cmp; grep-perl is called grep, the
name with which its messages begin) and tell grep-perl.js the name of its .wasm file
(../licenses/diffutils-build/, ../licenses/grep-perl-build/). base.js, the loader of the base
module, runs no program and is as downloaded.

One more change, in coreutils/8.32/date.js and gawk/5.1.0/gawk.js: the day of the year. These
loaders worked it out from the milliseconds that have passed since 1 January, local time. In a
zone with summer time that is one hour short in summer: for a local time between 00:00 and 00:59
on a summer day the result was the day before. GNU date then refused such dates
("date -d 2024-07-15" printed "invalid date" in the UK and in Europe), and %j could be a day
out. It is now the number of days between the two calendar dates. The script that makes the
change, and can check a file, is ../licenses/local-patches/fix-day-of-year.py.

3. WebAssembly programs
-----------------------
- GNU coreutils (17 programs) and GNU grep 3.7: one byte of each .wasm file is changed, which
  makes the C library's stdout unbuffered. Unchanged, these builds lose output that does not
  end with a newline ("seq 3 | tr '\n' ' '" printed nothing; "grep -lZ … | xargs -0 …" and
  "grep -z" printed nothing). The details, the byte in each file and the checksums of the files
  as downloaded are in coreutils/8.32/NOTICE.txt and grep/3.7/NOTICE.txt; the script is
  ../licenses/local-patches/unbuffer-stdout.py.
- GNU diffutils: diff and cmp were compiled for the course, from the release source; one line
  of cmp.c is changed (the word "byte" in its message). See diffutils/3.10/NOTICE.txt and
  ../licenses/diffutils-build/.
- GNU grep 3.11 with PCRE2 10.42 (grep-perl, which carries out "grep -P") was compiled for the
  course, from the two release sources, unchanged; one function that Emscripten's C library
  lacks (splice, which always fails) is added. See grep/3.11/NOTICE.txt and
  ../licenses/grep-perl-build/.
- base.wasm, gawk.wasm and sed.wasm are as downloaded from the Biowasm CDN. There are no .data
  files here.

What the page does around the programs – not changes to the programs
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(In assets/js/tools-wasm.js, unless another file is named.)
- cat is told when one of its input files is the file it writes to ("cat a b >> a",
  "cat a b > b"): it says "input file is output file", leaves that file out and ends with
  status 1, as GNU cat does. (The page checks this; the program cannot see that two names in the
  shared folder are one file.)
- tee /dev/stdout, tee /dev/stderr: the page makes the extra copy of the input (tee writes one
  more file, which is printed once more) – in a web page the program's standard output is a file,
  and two writers of one file would overwrite each other.
- The environment (see 1a): the variables that the shell exports, PWD, OLDPWD and _ as bash
  sets them. TMPDIR is left out unless it names a folder in the home folder (a program's own
  /tmp is not the /tmp of the terminal). cmp and diff are given en_US.UTF-8 where LANG, LC_ALL,
  LC_MESSAGES or LC_TIME is C.UTF-8: GNU cmp says "differ: char 7" when the language of the
  messages is C or POSIX and "differ: byte 7" otherwise, and diff -c dates its files
  "Tue Mar  5 12:34:56 2024" when the language of times is C or POSIX and
  "2024-03-05 12:34:56.000000000 +0000" otherwise; the C library of these builds (musl) takes
  C.UTF-8 for C in these respects, where Linux's (glibc) does not.
- wc is told when its input is a pipe, a here-document or a here-string (see 1a; bash hands a
  here-document over as a pipe when it has 64 KiB at most, as a file when it has more).
- date -r FILE gets the time from the page (the programs' copy of a file is newer than the file).
- A file that the page hands to the programs is given the time of its last change as the page
  shows it (ls -l, stat): the headers of "diff -u" and "diff -c" print the times of the two files.
  And a file that a program wrote has, in the page, the time at which the program wrote it. diff
  gets the clock of the time zone in TZ, as date does.
- grep -P is carried out by a second program: the Biowasm build of GNU grep 3.7 has no PCRE
  ("Perl matching not supported in a --disable-perl-regexp build"), so a grep command line that
  asks for Perl patterns – -P alone or in a group of letters (-oP, -oPm1), --perl-regexp; the
  page reads the options as grep's getopt does – goes to GNU grep 3.11 with PCRE2 10.42, built
  for the course (grep/3.11/ next to this file). Every other grep runs grep 3.7.
- A read-only file of the student's own (chmod -w, or a copy of an input: cp keeps the
  permissions) has mode 0444 in the programs' file system: a program cannot write into it
  ("Permission denied"), but it may put a new file in its place or remove it – sed -i does –,
  as on Linux, where that takes a folder one may write to, not a writable file.
- The time of a folder: when a program made, renamed or removed a name in a folder, the page
  takes the folder's new time from the shared file system (and sets it itself for what its own
  commands do) – "ls -td run_* | head -n 1", "find -newer", "[ dir -nt file ]".
- What is removed, copied or moved in the terminal (rm, cp, mv – done by the page) is carried out
  in the shared file system before the next program starts: files and folders that are gone are
  removed there too, and a copied or moved file gets its own bytes.
- A file that a program wrote is kept in the browser's storage (IndexedDB) a moment later, as the
  student's other files are (assets/js/project.js). If a program has to be stopped by force in
  the terminal, the programs are started afresh (their memory is lost) and those files come back
  from there (assets/js/terminal.js).
- While the AI agent runs a command, the page keeps copies of the files that programs wrote
  outside the agent's folder (in /keep of the base module's file system, where no program
  looks), and writes them back if the command changed or removed such a file; and it holds a
  copy of every file that programs wrote (up to 300 MiB, in its own memory), from which those
  files are written again if the programs have to be stopped by force during the command
  (assets/js/assistant.js). The copies are let go when the agent's run ends.
- Other absolute paths (/tmp/…) are inside the shared folder; in a program's messages and
  printed output they are shown as the student typed them (without the /shared/vfs prefix).
- Arguments that are no paths although they begin with a slash – the patterns and programs of
  awk, sed and grep, the delimiter of "cut -d /", the characters of "tr / _" – are given to the
  program as typed.
- A program without input of its own that stands in a block, a function or a script with
  redirected or piped input gets what is left of that input (see stdinPos above).
